Incubation temperatures profoundly influence early developmental trajectories in the Australian lungfish Neoceratodus forsteri. At a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], hatching occurs after a prolonged incubation period of 56 days [ab = 56 days]. In contrast, raising the temperature to 20 °C [T = 20 °C] markedly accelerates development, reducing the age at birth to 29 days [ab = 29 days]. A further increase to 25 °C [T = 25 °C] results in the shortest recorded hatching interval of just 16 days [ab = 16 days]. This strong thermal dependency underscores the species’ sensitivity to seasonal temperature variation in its native Queensland habitats. At the moment of hatching, newly emerged larvae possess a gut-free dry weight of 0.00165 grams , while their corresponding gut-free wet weight at birth is 0.00839 grams [Wwb = 0.00839 grams]. These minute initial masses reflect the substantial yolk reserves consumed during embryogenesis.

Juvenile growth under controlled laboratory conditions has provided detailed length-at-age data for this species. At a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], young individuals achieve a total length of 2.7 cm  by 110 days post-hatching. The sustained growth trajectory is characteristic of a long-lived vertebrate with a slow life-history pace, as individuals more than double their initial size by 240 days, reaching 6 cm  in total length under the same thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Ultimately, adult Neoceratodus forsteri can attain a formidable asymptotic size, with the ultimate total length recorded at 150 cm [Li = 150 cm]. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight for fully grown individuals is substantial, reaching 43000 grams [Wwi = 43000 grams]. Such a large body size is a notable trait among extant sarcopterygian fishes.

Reproductive maturation in Neoceratodus forsteri exhibits a clear sex-based dimorphism in both age and body length at first reproduction. At an environmental temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], females begin their first spawning after 22 years [tR = 22 years] of age, whereas males achieve their first reproduction considerably earlier, at 17 years [tR = 17 years] of age. This divergence is also reflected in body size; the total length at puberty for females is 83.5 cm [Lp = 83.5 cm], while males become reproductively capable at a smaller size of 77 cm [Lp = 77 cm] in total length. Such differences likely relate to the greater energetic demands of egg production and the need for a larger body cavity to accommodate developing oocytes. The age at first spawning is remarkably delayed compared to most teleost fishes, aligning with the species’ extreme longevity and low annual fecundity.

The maximum recorded longevity of Neoceratodus forsteri is exceptional among freshwater fishes, with a lifespan reaching at least 80 years [am = 80 years] when maintained at 20 °C at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. A well-known individual named Granddad, who resided at the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, was already present at that institution in 1933 and lived for over eight decades [am = over eight decades], providing direct empirical evidence for this extreme lifespan under captive conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Despite its large ultimate body size of 150 cm [Li = 150 cm] total length and 43000 grams [Wwi = 43000 grams] maximum wet weight, the species exhibits a low annual reproductive output. Females deposit approximately 600 eggs per spawning season [Ri = approximately 600 eggs per spawning season] with a spawning frequency of once per year [F_R_i = spawning frequency of once per year], reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high recruitment.

Comparative analyses with other lungfish species and ancient sarcopterygian lineages reveal several distinctive features. The eight-decade maximum lifespan realized by Granddad at the Shedd Aquarium (80 years) [am = 80 years], maintained at a stable 20 °C [T = 20 °C], aligns with the slow metabolic pace characteristic of these archaic fishes. The resulting ages at first spawning—22 years [tR = 22 years] at first spawning for females and 17 years [tR = 17 years] for males—are among the latest recorded for any fish species and are comparable to those of long-lived marine mammals at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The minute larval masses at emergence of 0.00165 grams  and 0.00839 grams [Wwb = 0.00839 grams] contrast dramatically with the adult maximum body weight of 43000 grams [Wwi = 43000 grams], reflecting a profound ontogenetic niche shift from a minute larva to a massive adult.
